newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU agrees new rules to control steel state aid.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees new rules to control steel state aid.

text.p: European Union industry ministers reached a compromise agreement on Thursday on new rules to control state support to the bloc's steel industry.
The new rules will take effect on January 1 next year and be in place until July, 2002.

Britain, Denmark, Sweden and the Netherlands had opposed the original proposal from the European Commission for a new steel state aid code due to fears it would weaken the rules on when governments could give support to ailing firms.
Britain in particular had insisted that the new code must be at least as tough as the one which runs out this year.
But British Industry Minister Greg Knight welcomed the compromise, saying it was much tougher than the Commission proposal.
"I am pleased that, after some hard negotiations, agreement has been reached on tight state aid to the steel industry," he said in a statement.

"It allows the steel industry to benefit from aid for projects such as research and development, environmental protection and closures, while protecting against subsidies whcih distort competition," he added.
An EU official said ministers reached a unanimous agreement after the text on the new rules had been tightened.
The ministers were under pressure to reach a deal soon as the current state aid code expires on December 31.
The rules on aid to the steel sector, which bans most state support, are now generally tougher than rules on support to other EU industries.

Among other things, the Commision proposal -- which was modified by ministers -- was intended to put the steel industry, still covered by the 1951 European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) Treaty, on the same footing as other sectors when it comes to research and environmental protection aid.
A further novelty was to allow closure aid also for "partial closures", for example the shutting down of one of a group's plants as long as there is a reduction in overall capacity.
The EU official said that under the agreed text, aid for partial closures could be granted but only under tight conditions.

In response to a request from Greece, ministers agreed that regional aid for investments of steel firms based in Greece could be allowed until the year 2000, provided that the total aid does not exceed 50 million European currency units ($63.5 million) and that production capacity is not increased.

Britain had feared that governments could use less stringent provisions on environmental aid to subsidise the creation of production plants if they could justify it in terms of environmental improvement.
London is very sceptical about state aid in general and fears aid in in the steel sector may hurt British Steel.
However, EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert had disputed this view, saying the Commission proposa would not relax the current rules.

If industry ministers had failed to agree, all cases of aid as from January 1 next year would have had to be vetted by the ministers, with all Commission decisions requiring their unanimous assent. ($1=0.79 Ecu)
